Hydrogen. Hydrogen, atomic number one and symbol H, is the lightest and most abundant chemical element in the universe, comprising roughly seventy-five percent of all ordinary matter by mass. At room temperature on Earth, hydrogen exists as a diatomic gas and is the fundamental building block of water, organic molecules, and fossil fuels. It is central to chemistry, astrophysics, and emerging clean-energy technologies.

Hydrogen has one proton and one electron. Its isotopes—deuterium with one neutron and tritium with two neutrons—are the only ones with special names.

Hydrogen forms single covalent bonds with nearly all elements, its behavior ranging from hydridic, or donation-like in metal hydrides, to cationic, losing the electron.

Hydrogen bonding between hydrogen and electronegative atoms—oxygen, nitrogen, and fluorine—creates weak but directional interactions essential to water's structure, protein folding, and DNA base-pairing.

In photosynthesis, hydrogen ions, or protons, are liberated from water during photolysis and accumulate in the thylakoid lumen, generating an electrochemical gradient that powers ATP synthesis.

Hydrogen combustion yields water and vast energy—approximately negative two hundred eighty-six kilojoules per mole for hydrogen plus one-half oxygen yielding water. It is the fuel of choice for space rockets and a candidate for carbon-free energy.

Hydrogen is the primary constituent of the Sun and stars, where it undergoes nuclear fusion under extreme pressure and temperature to produce helium and the energy that powers stellar luminosity.

Industrial Haber-Bosch synthesis converts nitrogen gas plus three hydrogen molecules to yield two ammonia molecules. This reaction fixes atmospheric nitrogen using hydrogen, enabling large-scale fertilizer production and modern agriculture.
